intro: Three camphors at the same shrine, spanning legend to living memory. The Living Gate is hollowed into a passage worshippers once walked through, put at 2,000 to 3,000 years old and revived after believers nearly killed it stripping its bark for a longevity charm. A few hundred metres away, Japan's first Prime Minister planted a camphor of his own in 1909. And facing the shrine's approach path stands the widest of the three, an eleven-metre-round camphor temple tradition credits to a legendary ancestor of the Ochi clan. All free, open at every hour, a short detour off the Shimanami Kaido.
meta_description: Ikiki no Gomon, the Living Gate: a camphor at Oyamazumi Shrine, Omishima, hollowed into a walkable passage. 2,000 to 3,000 years old. Free.
question_meta: Omishima's mapped tree is Ikiki no Gomon, the Living Gate camphor, put at 2,000 to 3,000 years old.
question_answer: Omishima's mapped tree is Ikiki no Gomon (The Living Gate), a camphor at Oyamazumi Shrine whose split and hollowed base forms a passage about two metres wide, three high and seven long, that worshippers walked through to reach the shrine's inner sanctuary. Its age is put at 2,000 to 3,000 years, a range that comes from two disagreeing sources rather than one measured figure.
question_context: The main trunk's circumference is eleven metres, the trunk union fifteen and a half, and the exposed root mass at ground level, the part the passage runs through, thirty two. Ages disagree by source: the standard reference work on the island gives 2,000 years, the on-site information board gives 3,000, and neither is tied to a dating method anyone can check. The tree nearly died in the Meiji era after believers stripped its bark for use as a longevity charm, and it recovered the only way a camphor can, throwing fresh growth from its own root base; that secondary trunk, four and a half metres round, now carries the crown while the original stands spent beside it. Ehime Prefecture designated it a Natural Monument in 1951, separate from the wider grove of camphors elsewhere on the shrine grounds that carries its own national designation. It stands five minutes on foot from Oyamazumi Shrine's main hall on Omishima Island, reached by car via the Shimanami Kaido or by bus from Imabari Station.

faq.q: What is special about this tree?
faq.a: Its hollowed, split base forms a natural passage that worshippers historically walked through on their way to Oyamazumi Shrine's inner sanctuary, which is where its name, the gate of the living tree, comes from.
Sources disagree: the standard local reference gives 2,000 years, the sign at the tree gives 3,000. Neither comes from a dating method that can be checked, so the honest answer is a wide range.
Yes, open year round with no set hours and no ticket needed.
By car via the Shimanami Kaido (about 10 minutes from Omishima IC to the shrine), or by bus from Imabari Station, about 65 minutes to the Oyamazumi Shrine stop plus a 5-minute walk.

faq.q: What other trees does Omishima map?
faq.a: Two more, both within the same shrine grounds: a camphor Japan's first Prime Minister, Ito Hirobumi, planted himself on 22 March 1909, and a third camphor standing on the shrine's approach path, its eleven-metre trunk credited by temple tradition to a legendary ancestor of the Ochi clan.

trees.name: Ikiki no Gomon (The Living Gate)

location.address: Oku-no-in (inner sanctuary) of Oyamazumi Shrine, Omishima, Imabari, Ehime Prefecture, Japan

trees.story:
There is a footpath through this tree. The split and hollowed base of the camphor forms a passage about two metres wide, three metres high and seven metres long, and worshippers walked through it on their way to the inner sanctuary of Oyamazumi Shrine. The name records exactly that: Ikiki no Gomon, the gate of the living tree.

How old it is depends on who you ask, and neither answer comes from a dating method anyone can check. The standard reference work on the island says 2,000 years. The board at the tree says 3,000. What has actually been measured is the size: eleven metres around the main trunk, fifteen and a half where the trunks meet, and thirty-two metres around the exposed root mass at ground level, which is the part you walk through.

It nearly died in the Meiji era, and its own believers were the reason. Bark taken from it was used as a charm for long life, stripped away until the original trunk was failing. The tree recovered the only way a camphor can, throwing fresh growth from its own root base. That second trunk, four and a half metres round, carries the crown today while the original stands spent beside it. One organism, regrown from itself.

Ehime Prefecture listed it as a Natural Monument in 1951. It sits five minutes from the shrine's main hall on Omishima, free and open at any hour, a short detour off the Shimanami Kaido.
trees.access: Free, open year round, no set hours. A public path/steps has been built through the hollow root passage itself. About a 5-minute walk from Oyamazumi Shrine's main hall; no dedicated parking at the site (nearest is the free municipal Fuji Park lot).
trees.transport: Omishima Island, reached by car via the Shimanami Kaido (Omishima IC, about 10 minutes to the shrine) or by bus from Imabari Station (approx. 65 minutes to the Oyamazumi Shrine stop, then a 5-minute walk).

trees.name: Ito Hirobumi Memorial Camphor

location.address: Oyamazumi Shrine, Miyaura, Omishima, Imabari, Ehime Prefecture, Japan

trees.access: Free, within the grounds of Oyamazumi Shrine, open daily.
trees.transport: On Omishima Island (Shimanami Kaido); same access as the shrine's other published tree (omi_001, Ikiki no Gomon), a few hundred metres away within the same shrine precinct.
trees.story:
Japan's first Prime Minister planted this one himself, which makes it the youngest tree of any consequence in a precinct where the others are counted in millennia.

Ito Hirobumi came to Oyamazumi Shrine on 22 March 1909, by tradition as a descendant of the Kono clan whose tutelary shrine this is. He put a camphor in the ground and he brushed the characters for the shrine's stone name-tablet on the same visit. Seven months later he was shot dead in Harbin.

The tree is about a metre round, which in this precinct counts as slender. Oyamazumi's grove was designated a National Natural Monument in 1951 as the oldest primeval camphor stand in Japan, and 38 named ancient camphors sit under that protection. This one is not among them and does not pretend to be. It is here for the date and the hand that planted it, not for its girth, and it is a rare thing anywhere: a tree whose first day is recorded to the morning.

That also makes it easy to walk past. No source places it more precisely than the shrine grounds, so the pin here marks the precinct rather than the trunk. Look for the young, straight camphor standing among the giants, a few hundred metres from the Living Gate. If you find it and can place it exactly, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by how slender it is, about a metre round, where the rest of the precinct's camphors are ancient. No source places it more precisely than the shrine grounds.

trees.name: Ochi-no-Mikoto's Hand-Planted Camphor
trees.age_estimate: roughly 2,600 years (temple tradition, not a measured date)

location.address: Approach path (sando) of Oyamazumi Shrine, Miyaura, Omishima, Imabari, Ehime Prefecture, Japan

trees.access: Free, within Oyamazumi Shrine grounds, open daily (same access as omi_001/omi_002).
trees.transport: Same as omi_001/omi_002: Omishima Island (Shimanami Kaido); by car or bus from Imabari Station.
trees.story:
A third camphor stands in the same shrine grounds, and it is the one visitors meet first. Ochi-no-Mikoto's Hand-Planted Camphor stands directly facing the sando, the approach path into Oyamazumi Shrine, with a trunk eleven metres round at breast height and a crown reaching fifteen metres over the path.

Temple tradition names Ochi-no-mikoto, a legendary ancestor of the later Ochi clan, as the one who planted it, sometime before the reign of Emperor Jinmu. That is a founding legend, not a documented planting date, and the site treats it that way: the age given, roughly 2,600 years, comes with the story attached rather than a growth-ring count.

What is measured is the girth. Japan's Ministry of Environment giant-tree survey for the Chugoku-Shikoku region puts it at eleven metres, among the thickest camphors recorded anywhere in the country. Together with Ikiki no Gomon and 35 further camphors across the grounds, it belongs to the Oyamazumi-jinja Camphor Grove, designated a National Natural Monument in 1951 as Japan's oldest primeval camphor stand.

Free to see, open daily, and the easiest of the shrine's three trees to find: it stands on the path everyone already walks, facing the gate.
